When two things adjoin, they are sitting directly next to each other and sharing a common boundary — a wall, a fence, a border line, or an edge. There is no gap between them. They are literally touching along one side.

Think of two puzzle pieces that fit together along one edge. They adjoin each other.
The single most important thing to understand

Adjoining ≠ merely nearby.

If two things are simply close to each other, they are not adjoining. To adjoin means the two things are in direct contact, sharing a physical boundary — a wall they both share, a fence line they both touch, or a border that belongs to both of them.

Two houses on the same street are near each other. Two houses that share a wall between them — like a semi-detached house — adjoin each other.
What kinds of things can adjoin?

Mostly physical spaces and areas:

  • Rooms — Two rooms in a building can adjoin if they share a wall and often a connecting door.
  • Buildings — A garage can adjoin a house if they share a common wall.
  • Properties / plots of land — Two plots adjoin if they share a boundary fence or line.
  • Countries / regions — France adjoins Germany because they share a national border. There is no other country in between them at that border.
  • Fields, gardens, parks — Any two areas of land that share an edge.

• "The bedroom adjoins the bathroom — you can walk directly from one into the other."
    → They share a wall, and there's a door connecting them.
  • "Our garden adjoins our neighbour's garden along the back wall."
    → The back wall is the shared boundary between the two gardens.
  • "Spain adjoins Portugal on its western side."
    → They share a national border along that side.
  • "The hotel room had an adjoining room, which was perfect for the family."
    → A second room directly connected to the first through a shared door in the shared wall.
  • "The two properties adjoin, so the owners often argue about the fence."
    → They share a boundary line, which is where the fence sits.
How it works in a sentence (without grammar jargon)

You can use "adjoin" in two natural ways:

Way 1 — One thing adjoins another thing:

"The kitchen adjoins the dining room."
(Kitchen → shares a boundary with → dining room)

Way 2 — Two things adjoin each other (or just "adjoin"):

"The two rooms adjoin." or "The two rooms adjoin each other."
(Both rooms share a boundary with the other)

Both ways are correct and common.

In real life, you will probably see the word adjoining (the adjective form) even more often than the verb itself. It means "directly next to and sharing a boundary with." It describes the thing that adjoins.

  • "An adjoining room" — a room that shares a wall/door with the room you're in.
  • "Adjoining fields" — fields that share a boundary edge.
  • "Adjoining properties" — land plots sharing a fence or boundary line.

You'll see "adjoining room" especially in hotels, where two rooms can be booked together and accessed through a shared door.

Near / close to: Just in the general vicinity. No direct contact required.

"The pharmacy is near the hospital" — they might be a street apart.
"The pharmacy adjoins the hospital" — they share a wall; they are in the same building complex.

Adjacent: Very similar to "adjoin," and often used interchangeably. However, "adjacent" can sometimes just mean "next to" without necessarily implying physical contact (e.g., "the adjacent seat" on a bus just means the seat beside you). "Adjoin" always implies a shared boundary — direct contact. So "adjoin" is the stricter, more precise word.

Abut: Practically a synonym of "adjoin." When one thing abuts another, it presses up against it along an edge. The two words are nearly identical in meaning. "Adjoin" is more common in general writing; "abut" appears more often in legal, architectural, and property contexts.

Border: Used more specifically for geographical areas — countries, states, regions. "France borders Spain" means the same as "France adjoins Spain." "Border" is more common in geographical and political contexts; "adjoin" is broader and works for rooms, buildings, and land too.
A mental image to lock it in

Imagine two sheets of paper lying flat on a table. You slide one sheet until its right edge touches the left edge of the other sheet perfectly — no gap, no overlap. At that moment, the two sheets adjoin each other. They share a common edge. That edge is their boundary.

Now scale that up: two rooms sharing a wall, two countries sharing a border, two gardens sharing a fence. That's what "adjoin" always describes.
To adjoin means to be directly next to something and share a common boundary — a wall, fence, or border — with no gap between the two things.
